claims.text: In-situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction can be used to monitor oxidation behavior in high-temperature materials.
In-situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction can be used to monitor phase stability in high-temperature materials.
HT-XRD directly tracks crystallographic changes during thermal exposure.
HT-XRD can directly detect the formation of crystalline oxide phases during thermal exposure.
The proposed initial sample is in a stable, unoxidized phase before exposure.
The sample is exposed to high-temperature oxidative conditions while diffraction data are collected simultaneously.
Oxidation is expected in an oxygen-rich atmosphere at temperatures above an example critical threshold of 700°C.
Oxidation produces oxide scales that can be detected by XRD.
Phase transitions are detectable through the appearance, shift, or intensity change of XRD peaks.
Thermally activated oxidation leads to the formation of new oxide phases.
Thermal exposure can cause phase transformations of the parent material.
Oxide formation and parent-phase transformations alter the diffraction pattern in a way that correlates with oxidation progression and structural evolution.
HT-XRD will reveal new diffraction peaks corresponding to oxide phases as oxidation proceeds.
HT-XRD will reveal shifts in parent-phase peaks as temperature increases.
The resolution of the XRD system and the oxidation rate can limit detection of rapid or subtle phase changes.
Phase-transition temperatures and kinetics vary with material composition.
HT-XRD may have uncertain sensitivity to minor phase changes and short-lived intermediates.

Failure to detect new peaks or significant diffraction-pattern changes under oxidation-inducing conditions would falsify the proposed effectiveness of HT-XRD for monitoring both oxidation behavior and phase stability.
